newCard.subject: History
newCard.name: Early First Nations and Inuit community life
newCard.description: Know a bounded repertoire of pre-1500 First Nation and Inuit community cases in what is now Canada. Identify each studied community and approximate period, describe supported food, shelter and material technologies, and explain particular connections to its local land, water and seasonal setting. Keep distinct communities and periods separate, and distinguish excavated remains, attributed interpretations and modern reconstructions.
evidence: After study, identify and broadly place one specific First Nation village and one early Inuit community in their different regions and approximate pre-1500 periods, rather than naming only broad present-day peoples.

Describe documented food, housing and material technologies in both studied cases, including a supported example of how local resources or seasonal conditions affected meeting needs. Use actual learned case facts rather than treating a generic Arctic or farming image as sufficient.

Use the learned knowledge to compare a supported similarity and difference, then respond to a changed-view or fresh attributed case detail without transferring another community’s practices or treating a modern reconstruction as an original period image.
newCard.assessmentPrompt: After learning about a mid-15th-century St Lawrence village and a 14th-century Inuit winter village, can {{name}} identify each place and period, describe its food, homes and tools, and explain one supported link to its setting? Compare the cases, then show a new labelled view or detail: can they connect it to the right case without assuming all communities lived alike?

pedagogy.summary: Teach actual named pre-1500 community knowledge with source and period attribution; existing history methods support but do not replace this knowledge.
bestPractices: Keep community, place and approximate period attached to every fact.
Use original paraphrases and lawfully accessed linked evidence; label modern reconstruction separately.
Compare documented needs/material solutions without ranking cultures or inventing universal social rules.
keyRepresentations: A broad locator and dated case strip.
Two separate food/home/material-technology profiles with source roles.
The actual 1992 Qariaraqyuk survey plan with its key and modern creation date.

learn.summary: Learn two bounded historical cases, explain supported setting relationships, and check factual retrieval across changed representations.

activities.title: Two named early community profiles
learnerActions: Locate each community broadly with two dated case cards; align c. 1300–1400 and c. 1450 without demanding exact year arithmetic or making archaeological labels modern citizenship categories.

Build separate food/home/material-technology profiles using actual supplied teaching facts. Connect one local resource/season to a supported need in each; compare farming/fishing/longhouse evidence with marine-harvest/storage/winter-house evidence. Avoid cultural ranking or climate determinism.

Contrast an excavated feature/artefact and a labelled modern reconstruction. Discuss what the source directly shows and where interpretation begins; this supports shared historical-evidence skills without pretending it supplies all archaeology methods.

After supported study and a delay, remove the fact captions and ask for meaningful case retrieval. Change the presentation/map view or give a fresh attributed feature and ask which learned case it fits and why. Keep a new case’s information supplied for transfer, not a demand to know untaught history.
activities.intendedInsight: Distinct communities met shared needs through particular learned practices and local material settings; archaeological source limits matter.
feedback: Which named place and period supports this fact?
Compare the actual case records instead of adding a universal people or gender rule.
Label the reconstruction and model limits before drawing another conclusion.
activities.rationale: Original low-confidence teaching design; no intervention/learner trial claimed.
sourceClaims: Parks Canada documents a mid-15th-century St Lawrence Iroquoian village with cultivated and gathered food evidence, longhouses/storage and ceramic, stone and bone objects.
The archaeological registry supports the named site setting, material features and bounded interpretations; source labels are retained rather than making a modern citizenship judgment.
The interpretation centre presents a modern reconstruction of the approximately 1450 village, not a surviving or photographed original 15th-century longhouse.
The MCA 2015 portrait describes its attributed interpretation and community advisory role; modern reconstruction photographs must remain labelled as such.

Whitridge’s excavated Qariaraqyuk case has substantial 14th-century occupation and material evidence of winter housing, marine harvesting/storage and access to nonlocal materials. Leadership/status reconstructions use explicitly limited archaeological and ethnographic modelling.

constraints: Prepare an original two-case fact/map/timeline packet from the cited sources. Provide clear dated labels, broad current place locators, an excavated-feature drawing/photo only through an authorized source/link, and an explicitly modern reconstruction view. Read source permissions before reproducing protected photos/text; original paraphrases and links suffice. Teach both case facts rather than hand over answers during the independent probe. A comparable verified pre-1500 case can replace a case only after its factual/identity/period boundaries are reviewed.

The initial repertoire includes both a dated First Nation village and a dated early Inuit community. An equivalent replacement must preserve actual community, period and region specificity and supported food, home and technology knowledge, not simply swap broad people labels.

Whitridge’s Qariaraqyuk social-leadership interpretation is an archaeological model using explicitly stated analogies; it is not an eyewitness constitution or universal Inuit political system. No unsupported child/gender/governance inventory is required by this card.
Other-society breadth, own-life comparison, government, conflict and sustained inquiry/map duties require separate source-fit task designs. The new claim does not make every source code Full.
No hunting/cooking/ceremonial reenactment, ancestry disclosure or exact-year arithmetic required.
Only factual-source checks are verified; teaching efficacy remains untested.
reviewNotes: 2026-11-10: original source-checked early-community knowledge draft. The actual MCA portrait, PDF pp. 47–48, was viewed; Qariaraqyuk published chapter site/dating evidence read. The actual figure 11.1, PDF p. 3 / printed p. 167, was viewed: a 1992 survey plan, not a pre-1500 map. Figure 11.3 is a research probable-exchange-route model, not a definitive historical itinerary. No modern Nation institution or later ethnographic role automatically backdated.

assess.correctAnswer: Recalls two distinct pre-1500 cases with actual food, home and technology facts, explains a supported setting relation, and separates period evidence from reconstruction.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Independent retrieval separates historical knowledge from caption copying; matched food/home needs across contrasting environments test factual distinctions rather than prestige or appearance. Changed views and source labels expose projection of one community or era onto another.
